milestones.label: Reaching the kindergarten entrance age

variesByState.note: Every state that sets a statewide entrance age sets the same one; what differs across states is the calendar cut-off date by which a child must reach it, and a handful of states leave that cut-off to local districts.

milestones.population: children entering public kindergarten in states that set a statewide entrance age
whatChanges: A child becomes eligible to enroll in public kindergarten once they reach the entrance age by the cut-off date their state sets.
Because cut-off dates differ across states, children born in the same month start kindergarten in different school years depending on where they live.
Some states leave the cut-off to local districts, and many allow waivers letting a child who misses it enroll early.

milestones.label: Compulsory school attendance begins

variesByState.note: The lowest state minimum applies in the states where the duty to attend begins at five; the highest applies in the single state where it begins at eight.

milestones.population: children in the fifty states and the District of Columbia, under each state's compulsory attendance statute
whatChanges: From this age a parent or guardian must enroll the child in school, or in an approved alternative such as private school or home instruction.
States differ in when the duty starts, so a family moving across state lines can find it begins earlier or later than where they lived.
Most states allow exemptions, including local district permission and conditions that make regular attendance impractical.

milestones.label: Compulsory school attendance ends

variesByState.note: The lowest state maximum applies in the states where the duty lifts at sixteen; the highest applies in the single state where it runs through nineteen.

milestones.population: children in the fifty states and the District of Columbia, under each state's compulsory attendance statute
whatChanges: Past this age a person is no longer legally required to attend school, whether or not they have completed a diploma.
Many states allow an earlier exit with parental consent, or once graduation requirements are met.
Free public education generally remains available past this age in most states, often for several more years.
